title: Leaders Who Confuse Being Liked With Being Respected
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article separates being liked from being respected, arguing many leaders wrongly assume affection is proof of good leadership because the signals of being liked are louder and easier to read than the signals of respect. Team members like leaders for warmth, kindness, and autonomy, but respect them for competence, consistency, fairness, and decisiveness -- distinct qualities that don't automatically travel together. The piece warns that chasing likeability over respect leads leaders to avoid hard decisions and tough conversations, and closes by arguing the best leaders build respect first, which naturally produces genuine likeability.
points: Because the signals of being liked are louder and faster to read than signals of respect, leaders often mistake one for the other.
People like leaders for warmth and autonomy but respect them for competence, fairness, and decisiveness -- different qualities entirely.
Prioritizing likeability leads leaders to avoid hard decisions, tough conversations, and accountability.
The best leaders insist on being respected first, which produces likeability as a byproduct rather than a goal.
quotes: Because the signals of being liked are louder, faster, and easier to read than the signals of being respected, leaders often mistake the visibility of fondness for respect, when this isn’t the case.
Team members respect leaders for what they stand for, how they think, and whether they can be trusted to be fair, consistent, and decisive.
A leader can be liked without producing any of the behaviors that make them respected. When likeability matters more than earning respect, leaders create a stew of ineffectiveness.
The good news is that strong leaders don’t have to choose between being respected and liked. The goal is to build respect in a way that naturally leads to healthy, genuine likeability.
Good leaders don’t chase approval. They build warm and meaningful relationships while earning trust through competence and consistency. Comfort attracts people, but competence keeps the trust.
